# Part 1: Data Cleaning and Preparation

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# --- Global chunk options ------------------------------------------------------
# These settings apply to all code chunks in the document:
#   - echo = FALSE      – hide R code from the rendered output
#   - message/warning   – suppress package startup messages and warnings
#   - comment = NA      – remove the leading "##" from console output
#   - fig.align/width   – centre figures and set a consistent size
#   - out.width = 100%  – make figures scale to the page width
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
	echo = FALSE,
	message = FALSE,
	warning = FALSE,
	comment = NA,
	fig.align = "center",
	fig.width = 10,
	fig.height = 5,
	out.width = "100%"
)

# Set the CRAN repository to avoid interactive prompts during package installation
options(repos = c(CRAN = "https://cloud.r-project.org"))

# --- Colour palette for genres -------------------------------------------------
# This named vector ensures that each genre always gets the same colour
# across all plots, regardless of the order in which genres appear.
# Any genre not listed here defaults to grey (#999999).
genre_palette <- c(
	Action = "#1f77b4",
	Adventure = "#ff7f0e",
	Comedy = "#2ca02c",
	Drama = "#9467bd",
	Horror = "#d62728"
)

# Helper function: maps a vector of genre names to the corresponding palette
# colour; unknown genres are assigned a neutral grey.
genre_color <- function(genres) {
	colors <- genre_palette[as.character(genres)]
	colors[is.na(colors)] <- "#999999"
	colors
}
```

## Load and verify the data

```{r}
# -- Load required package ------------------------------------------------------
# DT is used later for interactive tables (though not used in this part,
# it is required for the overall project; we check its presence here.)
if (!requireNamespace("DT", quietly = TRUE)) {
	stop("Package 'DT' is required. Install it once with: install.packages('DT', repos = 'https://cloud.r-project.org')")
}

# -- Read the raw CSV file ------------------------------------------------------
# The file is assumed to be in the working directory. We read it with
# stringsAsFactors = FALSE to keep character columns as strings for now.
movie_profit <- read.csv("movie_profit.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
# This makes missingness uniform across the whole dataset.
char_cols <- sapply(movie_profit, is.character)
movie_profit[char_cols] <- lapply(movie_profit[char_cols], function(x) {
  ifelse(trimws(x) == "", NA_character_, x)
})

# --- Basic dataset overview ----------------------------------------------------
# Compute simple dimensions and column type counts to get a first impression.
overview_table <- data.frame(
	Metric = c("Rows", "Columns", "Numeric columns", "Character columns"),
	Value = c(
		nrow(movie_profit),
		ncol(movie_profit),
		sum(sapply(movie_profit, is.numeric)),
		sum(sapply(movie_profit, is.character))
	)
)

knitr::kable(overview_table, caption = "Dataset overview")
```

## Check variable types and first 5 values

```{r}
# --- Inspect each variable's type and first few values -------------------------
# This helps to quickly identify columns that may need conversion (e.g. dates)
# and to detect any obvious formatting issues.
variable_overview <- data.frame(
	variable = names(movie_profit),
	type = sapply(movie_profit, function(x) class(x)[1]),
	first_5_values = sapply(movie_profit, function(x) {
		paste(head(x, 5), collapse = ", ")
	}),
	row.names = NULL
)

knitr::kable(variable_overview, caption = "Variable types and first 5 values")
```

## Convert release_date to Date type and check conversion results

```{r}
# --- Date conversion -----------------------------------------------------------
# The release_date column is read as character in MM/DD/YYYY format.
# We convert it to R's Date class using the appropriate format string.
release_date_raw <- movie_profit$release_date
movie_profit$release_date <- as.Date(release_date_raw, format = "%m/%d/%Y")

# --- Conversion summary --------------------------------------------------------
# Record the original and new classes, and count how many rows became NA
# after conversion (i.e. were invalid dates).
conversion_table <- data.frame(
	metric = c("Original type", "New type", "Invalid dates after conversion"),
	value = c(
		class(release_date_raw)[1],
		class(movie_profit$release_date)[1],
		sum(is.na(movie_profit$release_date) & !is.na(release_date_raw) & trimws(release_date_raw) != "")
	)
)

knitr::kable(conversion_table, caption = "release_date conversion summary")
```

## Check for missing values, duplicates, and logical consistency

```{r}
# --- Missing values ------------------------------------------------------------
missing_count <- colSums(is.na(movie_profit))
missing_pct   <- round(100 * missing_count / nrow(movie_profit), 2)
missing_summary <- data.frame(
  variable = names(missing_count),
  missing_count = as.integer(missing_count),
  missing_percent = missing_pct,
  row.names = NULL
)

# --- Duplicate rows ------------------------------------------------------------
# Check for exact duplicate rows; duplicates may arise from data entry errors.
dup_rows <- duplicated(movie_profit)
dup_count <- sum(dup_rows)

# --- Numeric column consistency ------------------------------------------------
# For the three financial columns, count negative values (should be none)
# and zero values (which may indicate missing or unreported data).
numeric_cols <- c("production_budget", "domestic_gross", "worldwide_gross")
neg_counts <- vapply(movie_profit[numeric_cols], function(x) sum(x < 0, na.rm = TRUE), integer(1))
zero_counts <- vapply(movie_profit[numeric_cols], function(x) sum(x == 0, na.rm = TRUE), integer(1))
numeric_checks <- data.frame(
  variable = numeric_cols,
  negative_values = neg_counts,
  zero_values = zero_counts
)

# --- Logical consistency: worldwide_gross should be >= domestic_gross ----------
# Since worldwide gross includes domestic, we expect no rows where
# worldwide_gross < domestic_gross. Such rows would indicate data errors.
bad_gross_count <- NA
if (all(c("domestic_gross", "worldwide_gross") %in% names(movie_profit))) {
	bad_gross_rows <- which(movie_profit$worldwide_gross < movie_profit$domestic_gross)
	bad_gross_count <- length(bad_gross_rows)
}

# --- Invalid dates after conversion (already computed, but shown again) --------
bad_date_count <- sum(
	is.na(movie_profit$release_date) &
		!is.na(release_date_raw) &
		trimws(release_date_raw) != ""
)

# --- Display all consistency tables --------------------------------------------
knitr::kable(missing_summary, caption = "Missing values by variable")

dup_table <- data.frame(
	metric = "Duplicate rows",
	count = dup_count
)
knitr::kable(dup_table, caption = "Duplicate row summary")

knitr::kable(numeric_checks, caption = "Numeric consistency checks")

logic_table <- data.frame(
	check = c("Rows where worldwide_gross < domestic_gross", "Invalid release_date values"),
	count = c(bad_gross_count, bad_date_count)
)
knitr::kable(logic_table, caption = "Logical consistency checks")
```

## Estimate impact of removing rows with missing values or gross = 0

```{r}
# --- Row-level missingness -----------------------------------------------------
# Before deciding on a cleaning strategy, we quantify how many rows would be
# removed under different filters. This helps us assess the trade‑off between
# data completeness and retaining sample size.

# Rows that contain at least one missing value (NA or empty string) in any column.
row_has_missing <- apply(movie_profit, 1, function(row) {
	any(is.na(row) | trimws(as.character(row)) == "")
})

# Rows where either domestic or worldwide gross is exactly zero.
# Zero gross may indicate missing data, unreported figures, or films with no
# theatrical release. For our analysis, we will exclude them because a log
# transformation would be undefined for zero, and they do not represent
# typical box-office behaviour.
gross_is_zero <-
	movie_profit$domestic_gross == 0 |
	movie_profit$worldwide_gross == 0

# Count overlaps and total rows that would be removed if we drop all such rows.
overlap_count <- sum(row_has_missing & gross_is_zero)
remove_all_count <- sum(row_has_missing | gross_is_zero)
total_movies <- nrow(movie_profit)
remove_all_pct <- round(100 * remove_all_count / total_movies, 2)

# --- Alternative: ignore missing values in mpaa_rating -------------------------
# The mpaa_rating column has a high proportion of missing values (as seen in
# the missing summary). If we choose to keep rows with missing rating but
# drop missing values elsewhere, we can retain more observations.
# We compute the removal count under this relaxed rule.
cols_except_rating <- setdiff(names(movie_profit), "mpaa_rating")
row_has_missing_no_rating <- !complete.cases(movie_profit[, cols_except_rating, drop = FALSE])

remove_no_rating_count <- sum(row_has_missing_no_rating | gross_is_zero)
remove_no_rating_pct <- round(100 * remove_no_rating_count / total_movies, 2)

# --- Impact summary table ------------------------------------------------------
impact_table <- data.frame(
	metric = c(
		"Rows with at least one missing value",
		"Rows with gross value 0 (domestic or worldwide)",
		"Overlap (missing and gross = 0)",
		"Rows removed (missing or gross = 0)",
		"Rows removed (ignoring missing mpaa_rating)"
	),
	count = c(
		sum(row_has_missing),
		sum(gross_is_zero),
		overlap_count,
		remove_all_count,
		remove_no_rating_count
	),
	percent = c(
		round(100 * sum(row_has_missing) / total_movies, 2),
		round(100 * sum(gross_is_zero) / total_movies, 2),
		round(100 * overlap_count / total_movies, 2),
		remove_all_pct,
		remove_no_rating_pct
	)
)

knitr::kable(impact_table, caption = "Impact of filtering rules")
```

## Remove rows with missing values (except rating) and gross = 0

```{r}
# --- Apply cleaning rules ------------------------------------------------------
# Based on the impact assessment, we choose to drop rows with:
#   1) missing values in any column except mpaa_rating (i.e., we keep
#      rows where only rating is missing), and
#   2) domestic_gross or worldwide_gross equal to zero.
#
# This decision balances data quality with sample size, as mpaa_rating is
# often missing but is not a critical variable for the main analyses.

cols_except_rating <- setdiff(names(movie_profit), "mpaa_rating")

# Identify rows with missing values outside of mpaa_rating
row_has_NA <- !complete.cases(movie_profit[, cols_except_rating, drop = FALSE])

# Identify rows with zero gross
gross_is_zero <-
	movie_profit$domestic_gross == 0 |
	movie_profit$worldwide_gross == 0

# Keep only rows that pass both conditions
movie_profit_clean <- movie_profit[!(row_has_NA | gross_is_zero), ]

# --- Cleaning summary ----------------------------------------------------------
cleaning_table <- data.frame(
	metric = c("Rows before cleaning", "Rows after cleaning", "Rows removed"),
	count = c(nrow(movie_profit), nrow(movie_profit_clean), nrow(movie_profit) - nrow(movie_profit_clean))
)

knitr::kable(cleaning_table, caption = "Cleaning summary")
```

# Part 2: Exploratory Data Analysis

## Overview

This document covers **Part 2 — Exploratory Data Analysis** of the Movie
Data Analysis project. The goal of EDA is to understand the dataset's
structure, distributions, and relationships before building any
statistical models.

The analysis proceeds in four broad steps:

1.  **Variable description** — what each column represents\
2.  **New derived columns** — at least 10 engineered features\
3.  **Descriptive statistics** — central tendency, spread, and outliers\
4.  **Visualisations** — 13 charts with explanations of what each one
    reveals

The cleaned dataset used here was produced in Part 1. It contains
`r nrow(movie_profit_clean)` movies spanning the genres Action,
Adventure, Comedy, Drama, and Horror.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 1 Variable description

The table below lists every column in the cleaned dataset, its data
type, and a short description of what it measures. Understanding the raw
variables is the essential first step before any transformation or
analysis.

```{r variable-description}
# Build a human-readable description for each original column
var_desc <- data.frame(
	variable = c(
		"X", "release_date", "movie", "production_budget",
		"domestic_gross", "worldwide_gross", "distributor",
		"mpaa_rating", "genre"
	),
	type = c(
		"integer", "Date", "character", "numeric",
		"numeric", "numeric", "character",
		"character", "character"
	),
	description = c(
		"Row index from the original CSV (not analytically meaningful)",
		"Date the film was released in US cinemas (MM/DD/YYYY → Date)",
		"Film title",
		"Reported production budget in USD",
		"Total box-office receipts from US/Canada markets in USD",
		"Total box-office receipts from all markets in USD",
		"Studio or distribution company releasing the film",
		"MPAA content rating (G, PG, PG-13, R, etc.); has missing values",
		"Primary genre as classified by the data source"
	),
	stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(var_desc, caption = "Original variables in the cleaned dataset")
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 2 Creating new derived columns

The original dataset provides budgets and gross revenues, but many
analytically interesting quantities — such as profitability or market
segments — must be computed. Below we create **12 new columns**
covering:

- financial indicators (international gross, ROI),\
- ranking flags (top-100 lists),\
- categorical groupings (budget bands, horror flag, movie type label),\
- scaled versions for display purposes.

```{r derived-columns}
movie_profit_enriched <- movie_profit_clean

# ── 1. International gross ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# The non-domestic portion of worldwide revenue. Useful for understanding
# how dependent a film's success is on the international market.
movie_profit_enriched$international_gross <-
	movie_profit_enriched$worldwide_gross - movie_profit_enriched$domestic_gross

# ── 2 & 3. ROI factors ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Return-on-investment expressed as a multiplier (e.g. 3.0 means the film
# earned 3× its production budget). We compute both a domestic and a
# worldwide version. Using a factor rather than a percentage makes it easy
# to say "this film returned 10× its budget."
movie_profit_enriched$roi_domestic_factor <- with(
	movie_profit_enriched,
	ifelse(production_budget > 0, domestic_gross  / production_budget, NA_real_)
)

movie_profit_enriched$roi_worldwide_factor <- with(
	movie_profit_enriched,
	ifelse(production_budget > 0, worldwide_gross / production_budget, NA_real_)
)

# ── 4 & 5. Top-100 flags ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Boolean flags marking whether a film ranks in the top 100 by domestic or
# international gross. These provide a simple, interpretable way to identify
# "blockbuster" films without choosing an arbitrary revenue threshold.
rank_domestic      <- rank(-movie_profit_enriched$domestic_gross,      ties.method = "first")
rank_international <- rank(-movie_profit_enriched$international_gross, ties.method = "first")

movie_profit_enriched$top100_domestic_gross      <- rank_domestic      <= 100
movie_profit_enriched$top100_international_gross <- rank_international <= 100

# ── 6. Horror flag ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# A logical column that is TRUE when the genre column contains "horror"
# (case-insensitive). This is the primary grouping variable for the
# Horror vs. Non-horror comparison that runs throughout the project.
movie_profit_enriched$is_horror_movie <-
	grepl("horror", movie_profit_enriched$genre, ignore.case = TRUE)

# ── 7. Movie type label ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# A readable character version of is_horror_movie, convenient for plot labels
# and table captions.
movie_profit_enriched$movie_type <-
	ifelse(movie_profit_enriched$is_horror_movie, "Horror", "Non-horror")

# ── 8. Budget band ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Binning production budgets into seven ordered categories allows us to
# compare how many films in each genre fall into each spending tier.
budget_breaks <- c(-Inf, 1e6, 5e6, 10e6, 20e6, 50e6, 100e6, Inf)
budget_labels <- c("< $1M", "$1M–$5M", "$5M–$10M",
                   "$10M–$20M", "$20M–$50M", "$50M–$100M", "> $100M")

movie_profit_enriched$budget_band <- cut(
	movie_profit_enriched$production_budget,
	breaks = budget_breaks,
	labels = budget_labels,
	right  = FALSE
)

# ── 9 & 10. Scaled financial columns (× $1,000) ───────────────────────────────
# Expressing large dollar amounts in thousands keeps the interactive table
# readable without sacrificing numeric sort order.
movie_profit_enriched$production_budget_k <- movie_profit_enriched$production_budget / 1000
movie_profit_enriched$domestic_gross_k    <- movie_profit_enriched$domestic_gross    / 1000
movie_profit_enriched$worldwide_gross_k   <- movie_profit_enriched$worldwide_gross   / 1000

# ── 11 & 12. Formatted date and release year ─────────────────────────────────
# A character column for display (ISO 8601) and an integer year used for
# time-series aggregations.
movie_profit_enriched$release_date_fmt <-
	ifelse(is.na(movie_profit_enriched$release_date), NA_character_,
	       format(movie_profit_enriched$release_date, "%Y-%m-%d"))

movie_profit_enriched$release_year <-
	as.integer(format(movie_profit_enriched$release_date, "%Y"))
```

**Summary of new columns**

| \# | Column | Type | Purpose |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|-------------------|
| 1 | `international_gross` | numeric | Revenue outside domestic market |
| 2 | `roi_domestic_factor` | numeric | Domestic gross ÷ production budget |
| 3 | `roi_worldwide_factor` | numeric | Worldwide gross ÷ production budget |
| 4 | `top100_domestic_gross` | logical | Top-100 film by domestic revenue |
| 5 | `top100_international_gross` | logical | Top-100 film by international revenue |
| 6 | `is_horror_movie` | logical | Genre contains "horror" |
| 7 | `movie_type` | character | Readable label ("Horror" / "Non-horror") |
| 8 | `budget_band` | factor | Seven ordered budget tiers |
| 9 | `production_budget_k` | numeric | Budget in thousands USD |
| 10 | `domestic_gross_k` | numeric | Domestic gross in thousands USD |
| 11 | `worldwide_gross_k` | numeric | Worldwide gross in thousands USD |
| 12 | `release_year` | integer | Calendar year of release |
